title: Recover a binomial experiment
stem: A binomial count has mean $6$ and variance $4$. Recover its parameters and explain why both moments are needed.
solution: For a nondegenerate binomial variable, $\mu=np$ and $v=np(1-p)$. Dividing gives $1-p=v/\mu=2/3$, hence $p=1/3$ and $n=18$. Both recovered parameters satisfy their domains. A mean of six alone admits infinitely many trial counts and probabilities, including $n=6,p=1$. The variance resolves that ambiguity within the binomial family; it does not prove that the unspecified experiment is binomial. Mutual independence, a fixed horizon and a common success probability must still be justified.

title: Reject impossible binomial moments
stem: Can a binomial variable have mean $3$ and variance $2$? Can it instead have mean $3$ and variance $5/2$? Also assess mean $3$ and variance $7/3$.
solution: The first pair gives $p=1-2/3=1/3$ and $n=3/(1/3)=9$, so it is feasible. The second gives $p=1-5/6=1/6$ and $n=18$, which is also feasible. Now compare mean three and variance $7/3$: they give $p=2/9$ and $n=27/2$, which is not an integer, so that pair is impossible in the ordinary binomial family. Checking only $0\le v\le\mu$ is necessary but insufficient. The implied trial count must be a nonnegative integer.

title: A parameter from neighboring masses
stem: For $X\sim Bin(8,p)$, suppose $P(X=3)=2P(X=2)>0$. Find $p$ and the modes.
solution: The ratio is $\frac{P(X=3)}{P(X=2)}=\frac{8-2}{3}\frac p{1-p}=2\frac p{1-p}$. Thus $p/(1-p)=1$, giving $p=1/2$. Since $(n+1)p=9/2$ is not an integer, the unique mode is its floor, four. The positivity assumption rules out endpoint cases where division by a zero mass would be invalid. The ratio uses adjacent counts and the fixed value of $n$; comparing masses separated by several indices requires a product of ratios.

title: Tied binomial modes
stem: Find all modes of $X\sim Bin(9,2/5)$ and justify the tie rather than rounding its mean.
solution: The ratio from $k$ to $k+1$ equals $(9-k)2/[3(k+1)]$. It exceeds one for $k<3$, equals one at $k=3$, and is below one afterward. Therefore counts three and four are both modes. Equivalently, $(n+1)p=4$ is an integer, producing modes three and four. The mean is $18/5$, whose nearest integer happens to be four but would lose the equally probable count three. The mode is a maximizer of probability mass, not an estimate obtained by rounding expectation.

title: A fair-count strict threshold
stem: Eight fair independent coins are tossed. Find the probability of fewer than four heads without adding four separate binomial terms.
solution: Reflection exchanges heads and tails, so $P(X<4)=P(X>4)$. The central mass is $P(X=4)=\binom84/2^8=70/256$. The remaining probability splits equally, giving $P(X<4)=(1-70/256)/2=93/256$. Fewer than four excludes the central count; at most four would add $70/256$. The symmetry argument requires a fair coin. It would not justify equal tails for a biased success probability, even if the threshold were located near the mean.

title: Parity from a PGF
stem: For $X\sim Bin(5,1/3)$, find $P(X\text{ is even})$ and explain the role of evaluation at minus one.
solution: Write $e=P(X\text{ even})$ and $o=P(X\text{ odd})$. Then $e+o=G(1)=1$ and $e-o=G(-1)=(2/3-1/3)^5=1/243$. Solving gives $e=(1+1/243)/2=122/243$. The alternating signs select parity because $(-1)^k$ is positive at even indices and negative at odd indices. This method sums all admissible even masses at once. It is valid for a probability generating function at minus one; it is not a claim that a negative number is a probability.

title: Condition on a fixed total
stem: Six independent Bernoulli trials have common $0<p<1$. Given exactly two successes in all six, find the probability of exactly one success among the first three.
solution: Every two-success set has the same unconditional weight $p^2(1-p)^4$, so conditioning makes the $\binom62=15$ sets uniform. To obtain one success in each half, choose one position from each three-position block, giving nine sets. The probability is $9/15=3/5$. The conditional first-half count is hypergeometric, not an independent binomial with probability $1/3$. The value of $p$ cancels because all conditioned configurations share it; unequal trial probabilities would destroy the uniform-set conclusion.

title: Thinning a fixed count
stem: Each of six objects independently qualifies with probability $2/3$. Each qualified object independently passes with probability $1/2$. Find the final count law, mean and variance.
solution: Combine qualification and passing at the object level. A final success requires both events and has probability $(2/3)(1/2)=1/3$. Independence across objects gives $Y\sim Bin(6,1/3)$, with mean two and variance $6(1/3)(2/3)=4/3$. Alternatively, condition on the qualification count $K$ and use $E[z^Y\mid K]=((1+z)/2)^K$ in its binomial PGF. Replacing $K$ by its mean four and using $Bin(4,1/2)$ preserves the mean but gives the wrong variance and support.

title: Classify successes into competing labels
stem: In five independent trials, an A outcome has probability $1/4$, a B outcome probability $1/2$, and otherwise neither occurs. Find the covariance of their counts and $P(A=1,B=2)$.
solution: Within a trial, the A and B indicators cannot both equal one, so their covariance is $0-(1/4)(1/2)=-1/8$. Across different trials they are independent; summing gives $Cov(A,B)=-5/8$. For the joint event, choose one A position and two B positions; the remaining two are neither. Thus the probability is $\frac{5!}{1!2!2!}(1/4)(1/2)^2(1/4)^2=15/128$. Binomial marginals do not imply independent counts. Multiplying their marginal probabilities would count impossible overlapping labels.

title: Third factorial moment and ordinary third moment
stem: For $X\sim Bin(7,2/5)$, derive $E[X^3]$ without expanding seven indicators cubically.
solution: The PGF derivative gives $E[X(X-1)(X-2)]=7\cdot6\cdot5(2/5)^3=336/25$. Likewise $E[X(X-1)]=7\cdot6(2/5)^2=168/25$ and $E[X]=14/5$. The identity $X^3=X(X-1)(X-2)+3X(X-1)+X$ therefore gives $E[X^3]=336/25+504/25+70/25=182/5$. The falling-factorial moment differs from the ordinary moment. Omitting the lower-order corrections would lose repeated-index terms in a direct indicator expansion.

title: A zero-truncated binomial law
stem: For $X\sim Bin(4,1/2)$, compute $E[X\mid X>0]$ and $Var(X\mid X>0)$.
solution: The conditioning probability is $15/16$. Since the excluded value is zero, the first and second raw numerator moments remain $E[X]=2$ and $E[X^2]=Var(X)+E[X]^2=5$. Thus the conditional moments are $32/15$ and $16/3$. Subtract their squared mean to obtain $16/3-1024/225=176/225$. Dividing the unconditional variance by $15/16$ is wrong because conditional variance must use the conditional center. The positive-conditioned law has support one through four and is not an ordinary binomial law.

title: Unequal independent trial probabilities
stem: Three independent trials have success probabilities $1/2,1/3,1/4$. Find the full success-count law and compare its variance with a same-mean binomial law.
solution: Multiply $(1+z)/2$, $(2+z)/3$ and $(3+z)/4$. Their numerator is $6+11z+6z^2+z^3$, so the masses at zero through three are $1/4,11/24,1/4,1/24$. The mean is $13/12$ and variance $1/4+2/9+3/16=95/144$. The same-mean binomial would have $p=13/36$ and variance $3p(1-p)=299/432$, exceeding $285/432$ by $7/216$. Equal mean does not identify equal laws. The difference measures probability heterogeneity, not dependence.

title: Pairwise independence is insufficient
stem: Let $U,V$ be independent fair bits, and let $W=U\operatorname{xor}V$. Is $U+V+W$ binomial? Find its law.
solution: The four equally likely pairs $(U,V)$ produce triples $000,011,101,110$. Every two coordinates are independent fair bits, but all three are not mutually independent: their parity is always even. The sum is zero with probability $1/4$ and two with probability $3/4$. Its mean is $3/2$ and variance $3/4$, the same as $Bin(3,1/2)$, yet its support excludes one and three. This counterexample simultaneously disproves inferring a binomial law from pairwise independence or from matching its first two moments.

title: A common hidden success probability
stem: Before six trials, choose $P=1/4$ or $3/4$ with equal probabilities. Conditional on P, the trials are independent. Find the count mean, variance and all-zero probability.
solution: The average success probability is $1/2$ and $Var(P)=1/16$. Total variance gives $Var(S)=6(1/2)(1/2)+6\cdot5/16=27/8$, while the mean is three. The all-zero mass is $\frac12[(3/4)^6+(1/4)^6]=365/4096$. A fair binomial would have variance $3/2$ and all-zero mass $1/64$. Conditional independence does not imply unconditional independence when trials share P. The excess variance quantifies the shared-parameter contribution; it is not numerical error.

title: Reflect a biased binomial event
stem: For $X\sim Bin(10,1/5)$, express $P(X\ge8)$ as a lower-tail event for another binomial variable. Why is reflecting around the mean invalid?
solution: Count failures instead of successes: $Y=10-X\sim Bin(10,4/5)$. The event $X\ge8$ is exactly $Y\le2$, so its probability is $\sum_{j=0}^2\binom{10}j(4/5)^j(1/5)^{10-j}$. Reflection changes the success parameter from $p$ to $1-p$ and the threshold from eight to two. It does not assert symmetry of the original biased distribution. Its mean is two, but masses equally spaced around that mean need not agree.

title: Distribution of the first successful position given a count
stem: Ten common-probability independent trials contain exactly three successes. Given this total, find the probability that the first success is at position four.
solution: Conditioning produces a uniform three-position subset of ten. Having the first success at four forces positions one through three to fail and position four to succeed. Choose the remaining two successes among positions five through ten, giving $\binom62$ configurations out of $\binom{10}3$. The probability is $15/120=1/8$. The unconditioned first-success law would be geometric, but the given total changes the law and bounds its support. This is an order statistic of a uniform subset, connecting conditional binomial positions to finite-population waiting.

title: Positive waiting versus failure count
stem: A first-success waiting variable T has mean six. Identify p, $E[T^2]$, $Var(T)$ and the mean of the number F of preceding failures.
solution: For positive geometric waiting, $E[T]=1/p$, so $p=1/6$ and $q=5/6$. Its variance is $q/p^2=30$. Hence $E[T^2]=30+36=66$. The failure count is $F=T-1$, giving mean five and the same variance thirty. Subtracting one changes the mean and support but not variance. If the symbol T instead denoted failures, mean six would imply $p=1/7$; identifying the convention before solving is essential.

title: A shifted conditional wait
stem: For positive $T\sim Geom(1/3)$, find $P(T>10\mid T>7)$ and $E[T\mid T>7]$.
solution: The survival probability is $P(T>m)=(2/3)^m$. The ratio is $(2/3)^{10}/(2/3)^7=(2/3)^3=8/27$. Conditional on the first seven failures, the remaining wait has the original positive geometric law. Thus $E[T\mid T>7]=7+3=10$. This expectation includes seven elapsed trials; it is not the residual expectation three. Writing $T\ge7$ instead would condition on only six guaranteed failures and change both thresholds.

title: A strict threshold with a noninteger bound

title: Cap a wait without dropping failures
stem: For $T\sim Geom(1/2)$ on positive integers, define $C=\min(T,4)$. Find its law and mean.
solution: The masses at one, two and three remain $1/2,1/4,1/8$. At four, combine an actual fourth-trial success with every later success: $P(C=4)=P(T\ge4)=1/8$. The mean is $1/2+2/4+3/8+4/8=15/8$. The tail-sum identity gives the independent check $E[C]=\sum_{j=0}^3(1/2)^j=15/8$. Assigning only $P(T=4)=1/16$ to the endpoint loses the probability of unresolved attempts. Capping records all attempts and differs from success-only truncation.

title: A failure code at zero
stem: Let R equal T when $T\le4$ and zero otherwise, for positive $T\sim Geom(1/2)$. Find its mean and explain why R is not a failure-count geometric variable.

title: A geometric parity event
stem: For positive $T\sim Geom(p)$, derive the probabilities of odd and even waiting times. Evaluate at $p=1/3$.
solution: Odd positions have masses $p,pq^2,pq^4,\ldots$, so their sum is $p/(1-q^2)=1/(1+q)$. Even positions add one failure factor, giving $q/(1+q)$. At $p=1/3$, the probabilities are $3/5$ and $2/5$. A parity probability is generally not one half, even though both parity classes contain infinitely many integers. The earliest positions receive larger mass. The series calculation requires $p>0$; at $p=0$ there is no finite successful waiting time.

title: Two clocks and a tie
stem: Independent positive geometric waits have success probabilities $1/3$ and $1/2$. Find the probabilities that the first is smaller, they tie, and the second is smaller.
solution: At position k, a strict first-clock win has probability $p_1q_1^{k-1}q_2^k$. Summing gives $p_1q_2/(1-q_1q_2)$. Here the denominator is $2/3$, so the first-clock win probability is $1/4$. A tie has probability $p_1p_2/(1-q_1q_2)=1/4$. The second-clock win is $p_2q_1/(1-q_1q_2)=1/2$. These disjoint events sum to one. Treating a discrete race as a continuous one would omit a nonzero tie probability.

title: Minimum and maximum waits
stem: For the two independent waits in the preceding race, compute the expectations of their minimum and maximum.
solution: The minimum survives m trials only when both clocks do, so its survival is $(q_1q_2)^m=(1/3)^m$. It is positive geometric with success probability $2/3$, giving mean $3/2$. Pointwise, the minimum plus the maximum equals the sum of the two waits. Their individual means are three and two, hence the maximum has mean $5-3/2=7/2$. The maximum is not geometric: its survival is $q_1^m+q_2^m-(q_1q_2)^m$. Independence is needed for the product survival, not for the pointwise sum identity.

title: Waiting with changing hazards
stem: On trial i, an independent attempt succeeds with probability $p_i=1/(i+1)$. Find $P(T>m)$ and decide whether the first-success wait has finite mean.
solution: Independence gives $P(T>m)=\prod_{i=1}^m(1-p_i)=\prod_{i=1}^m i/(i+1)=1/(m+1)$. This survival tends to zero, so success eventually occurs almost surely. However, the positive-integer tail-sum mean is $\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}1/(m+1)$, which diverges. Almost-sure finite completion therefore does not imply finite expected duration. The hazards change with elapsed trials, so neither a constant-p geometric law nor its memoryless formula applies.

title: A mixture destroys memorylessness
stem: Choose p equally from $1/4,3/4$ once, and then wait for a success in conditionally independent trials. Compare $P(T>2\mid T>1)$ with $P(T>1)$.
solution: The initial one-trial survival is the average failure probability, $1/2$. Two-trial survival averages squared failure probabilities: $\frac12[(3/4)^2+(1/4)^2]=5/16$. Therefore conditional residual one-trial survival is $(5/16)/(1/2)=5/8$, not $1/2$. Observing a failure increases posterior weight on the low-success regime. Conditional geometric behavior given p does not establish an unconditional geometric law. The same hidden parameter persists through the experiment; choosing a fresh independent p each trial would have a different result.

title: Recover a geometric law from memorylessness
stem: A positive-integer variable T satisfies $P(T>m+n)=P(T>m)P(T>n)$ for all nonnegative integers. If $P(T>1)=3/5$, derive its full law.

Taking successive survival differences produces $P(T=k)=(3/5)^{k-1}(2/5)$ for positive k. Thus T is geometric with success probability $2/5$. Its mean is $5/2$. The support and the survival identity establish the law; knowing a single tail probability alone would not suffice.

title: The final-success coefficient

title: Failure-based negative-binomial moments

title: An independent sum with a common parameter

title: Tied negative-binomial modes
stem: For the failure count before three successes with $p=1/3$, find all modes.
solution: The ratio of masses at f plus one and f is $q(f+r)/(f+1)=2(f+3)/[3(f+1)]$. It equals one when f equals three, exceeds one at smaller indices and is below one at larger indices. The failure-count mode formula involves $(r-1)q/p$; its integral value creates a tie one count earlier. Applying a binomial mode rule to this unbounded stopped count is invalid.

title: A conditional residual wait after a partial count

title: The second moment of a stopped wait
stem: For the total wait T through four successes with $p=2/3$, find $E[T^2]$ and the covariance of T with its failure count F.
solution: The mean is $r/p=6$, and variance is $rq/p^2=4(1/3)/(4/9)=3$. Consequently $E[T^2]=3+36=39$. Since $F=T-4$, covariance is $Cov(T,F)=Cov(T,T-4)=Var(T)=3$. The same random variable shifted by a constant is perfectly positively correlated when variance is nonzero. T and F are not independent merely because one counts all trials and the other only failures. Their deterministic relation should be used before attempting a joint probability calculation.

title: A binomial horizon mistaken for a stopping horizon
stem: An observer reports exactly three successes in ten trials with probability p. Another observer reports the third success occurring at trial ten. Compare their event probabilities.
solution: The fixed-horizon event has probability $\binom{10}3p^3q^7$. The stopped event forces the tenth trial to be a success and chooses the other two among the first nine, giving $\binom92p^3q^7$. Their ratio is $\binom92/\binom{10}3=3/10$, independent of p when both probabilities are positive. Given exactly three successes among ten, each of the three success positions is uniformly distributed over the ten positions, so the final trial is successful with probability $3/10$. The distinction is a support and combinatorial constraint, not a change in trial probability.

title: Success before a failure budget is exhausted
stem: With success probability $2/3$, stop when either three successes or two failures have occurred. Find the probability that the successes win.
solution: Successes win exactly when the third success occurs with zero or one preceding failures. The two probabilities are $p^3$ and $\binom31p^3q$, totaling $p^3(1+3q)=16/27$. Equivalently, among the first four trials at least three are successes, whose binomial probability is $4p^3q+p^4=16/27$. The event equivalence works because either stopping condition must occur within four trials. Continuing after a losing second failure and counting later successes would change the experiment.

title: An exponential tilt of a geometric law
stem: Let F have failure-based geometric parameter p. Reweight its masses by $a^f$ with $a\ge0$. When does normalization exist, and what is the resulting law?
solution: The unnormalized weights are $p(aq)^f$. Their sum is $p/(1-aq)$ exactly when $aq<1$. Dividing gives masses $(1-aq)(aq)^f$, a failure-based geometric law with new success parameter $1-aq$. At $a=0$, all mass is at zero; when $aq\ge1$ the sum diverges and no normalized probability law exists. The tilt changes the distribution of the entire count. This algebra explains geometric posterior updates under an exponentially decreasing likelihood, without treating a likelihood itself as a normalized prior.

title: A full hypergeometric probability
stem: Three items are sampled uniformly without replacement from ten, of which four are marked. Find the probability of exactly two marks, the mean and variance.
solution: There are $\binom{10}3=120$ equally likely subsets. Favorable subsets choose two of four marks and one of six unmarked items, giving $6\cdot6=36$, so the probability is $3/10$. The mean is $3(4/10)=6/5$. Variance includes the finite-population factor: $3(4/10)(6/10)(7/9)=14/25$. Replacement would instead give binomial variance $18/25$ and a different mass at two. Uniform subsets and replacement assumptions must be established before applying either model.

title: Find the effective support first

title: Draw the whole population
stem: A hypergeometric experiment samples all N objects from a population with K marks. What becomes of its mean, variance and mass formula, including $N=1$?

The subset probability is one at K because the full population has only one possible sample. title: Count marked items left behind

Its mean is $K-nK/N=(N-n)K/N$ and its variance equals that of X because subtraction from a constant leaves variance unchanged. title: A conditional independent-binomial pair
stem: Independent $A\sim Bin(4,p)$ and $B\sim Bin(6,p)$ share $0<p<1$. Find $P(A=2\mid A+B=3)$.

Choosing two positions from the four A positions and one from the six B positions gives $\binom42\binom61/\binom{10}3=36/120=3/10$. Direct cancellation of $p^3q^7$ in the joint-to-total ratio yields the same result. The conditional A law is hypergeometric. title: Compare replacement and depletion
stem: For sample size n from N with mark fraction p, compare the variance with and without replacement. What happens when n is one and when n is N?

At n equal to one, the variances agree because no preceding draw can have depleted the population. At n equal to N, the without-replacement count is constant, while replacement remains random if $0<p<1$. title: Identify a hypergeometric mode

title: A finite-population success wait
stem: Randomly order seven items, of which three are marked. Let T be the position of the second mark. Find its support, $P(T=4)$, mean and variance.

title: Last marked position
stem: Four marked items are randomly positioned among ten slots. Find the expected position of the last mark and the expected number of unmarked slots after it.

title: Derive finite-wait gap covariance
stem: In a uniform arrangement of K marks and M unmarked items, let $G_0,\ldots,G_K$ be the unmarked gaps. Derive their pair covariance from symmetry and fixed sum.

The fixed-sum identity determines covariance after the one-gap variance is known; it does not imply independent gaps.

title: Translate a Poisson rate into exposure

title: Recover a Poisson parameter from a ratio

title: A Poisson parity identity
stem: For $X\sim Pois(\lambda)$, derive the even-count probability and evaluate it at $\lambda=1$.
solution: The PGF is $G(z)=\exp(\lambda(z-1))$. At z equal to minus one it gives $E[(-1)^X]=e^{-2\lambda}$, the difference between even and odd probabilities. Together with their sum one, this yields $P(X\text{ even})=(1+e^{-2\lambda})/2$. At parameter one the answer is $(1+e^{-2})/2$. The expression approaches one half as the parameter grows but exceeds it for every finite positive parameter. Counting infinitely many even and odd indices does not assign equal total probability.

title: A Poisson fourth moment
stem: Derive $E[X^4]$ for a Poisson variable of parameter $\lambda$.
solution: The factorial moments are $E[(X)_j]=\lambda^j$. Expand the polynomial as $X^4=(X)_4+6(X)_3+7(X)_2+X$, which can be checked by expanding each falling factorial. Therefore $E[X^4]=\lambda^4+6\lambda^3+7\lambda^2+\lambda$. The derivative order and the ordinary exponent cannot be interchanged: the fourth PGF derivative at one gives only the fourth falling-factorial moment. At parameter zero every term vanishes, consistent with a constant zero variable. This method avoids an infinite direct sum while retaining repeated-index corrections.

title: Unconditional Poisson splitting
stem: A Poisson count has parameter six. Independently label each event A with probability $1/3$ and B otherwise. Find the joint PGF and covariance of the two counts.

title: Equal mean and variance do not identify Poisson
stem: A variable takes values zero and two with equal probabilities. Compare it with a Poisson law using its first two moments and its support.

A Poisson law with parameter one has the same first two moments, but it assigns positive probability to every nonnegative integer, including one, which this variable never takes. title: A zero-truncated Poisson count

Subtraction gives $Var(X\mid X>0)=\lambda/d-\lambda^2e^{-\lambda}/d^2$. This law has positive support and differs from simply adding one to an ordinary Poisson variable. For tiny lambda, stable computation of d is needed; mathematically the conditioned distribution approaches a point mass at one as lambda tends to zero.

title: Size bias changes a count law
stem: An observed Poisson count is sampled with probability proportional to its count, so its new PMF is $kP(X=k)/E[X]$. Identify the resulting distribution for positive parameter.
solution: The size-biased mass at positive k is $k e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/(k!\lambda)=e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{k-1}/(k-1)!$. Hence the observed variable equals one plus a Poisson variable of the same parameter. Its mean is $1+\lambda$ and variance lambda. The zero mass disappears because a zero-count object cannot be selected by this rule. title: A finite sum is not a scaled copy

title: Prove the one-coordinate coupling distance

title: A fixed-k limit is not uniform over moving k

title: Shared dependence can break rare-event reasoning

title: A small-interval process statement

title: A random-sum model
stem: A Poisson number N of parameter two determines how many independent fair Bernoulli marks are summed. Find the resulting count law and distinguish this from $NB$ for a single common mark.
solution: Independent fresh marks give PGF $G_N((1+z)/2)=\exp(z-1)$, so the result is Poisson with parameter one. A single common fair mark B instead yields a mixture: zero if B is zero and the entire Poisson count if B is one. Its zero probability is $(1+e^{-2})/2$, not $e^{-1}$, and its variance is two rather than one. Random-sum composition requires independent summands and independence of the summands from N; repeating the same mark creates dependence.

title: Conditional law under a zero observation
stem: A failure-based geometric family-size prior has parameter one half. Each child independently passes an observation test with probability one half. Given zero passing children, derive the posterior family-size law.
solution: The prior mass at n is $2^{-n-1}$ and the likelihood of zero passes is $2^{-n}$. Their product is $(1/2)4^{-n}$. The sum over all nonnegative n is $2/3$, so the posterior mass is $(3/4)(1/4)^n$, a failure-based geometric law of parameter $3/4$. Its positive-size probability is $1/4$ and mean $1/3$. The zero-size case satisfies the observation automatically and must be retained. Updating individual outcomes without reweighting family sizes misses the selection effect.

title: Why factorial moments do not justify an arbitrary law
stem: An investigator knows $E[X]=2$ for an integer count but assumes $E[X(X-1)]=4$ because a Poisson variable has that value. Diagnose the inference and give a counterexample.
solution: A Poisson variable of mean two does have second falling-factorial moment four. However, the constant count X equal to two has the same mean and falling-factorial moment two, not four. Its variance is zero rather than two. The identity $E[X^2]=E[X(X-1)]+E[X]$ holds for any variable with finite second moment; substituting a Poisson-specific factorial moment requires establishing the Poisson law first. A mean is an expectation constraint, not a generating-function or full-distribution specification.

title: Choose the family before calculating
stem: Classify three experiments: successes in eight independent attempts with common p; attempts through the third success; and marks among eight objects drawn without replacement from a finite population.
solution: The first is a fixed-horizon binomial count with support zero through eight. The second is a total-trial negative-binomial wait with support three onward when $0<p<1$; its last attempt must succeed. The third is hypergeometric with support bounded by both marked and unmarked pools. The number eight names different quantities in the first and third experiments, and there is no deterministic eight-attempt horizon in the second. Correct classification precedes selecting a coefficient, moment formula or tail expression.

title: Conditioning on an impossible event
stem: For $X\sim Bin(4,0)$, can one calculate $P(X=1\mid X>0)$ by continuity from positive p? Is that an ordinary conditional probability in the stated experiment?
solution: At p equal to zero, X is identically zero and $P(X>0)=0$. The usual finite-event conditional ratio is therefore undefined. For positive p, the conditional probability is $4p(1-p)^3/[1-(1-p)^4]$, whose limit is one as p approaches zero. That limiting conditional law is a different construction and must be labeled as such. An algebraic limit does not assign a uniquely determined event conditional within a model where the conditioning event has zero probability.

title: A Poisson count conditioned by a parity observation
stem: For positive $\lambda$, derive $E[X\mid X\text{ even}]$ when X is Poisson.
solution: Use $E[X(-1)^X]=(-1)G^{\prime}(-1)=-\lambda e^{-2\lambda}$. Since the even indicator equals $(1+(-1)^X)/2$, the even-conditioned first-moment numerator is $\lambda(1-e^{-2\lambda})/2$. Divide by the even probability $(1+e^{-2\lambda})/2$ to obtain $\lambda(1-e^{-2\lambda})/(1+e^{-2\lambda})$. The support contains only even integers, so the conditional law is not Poisson even though its calculation uses the original PGF. Differentiating at minus one requires the extra z factor for $E[Xz^X]$.

title: A binomial sample conditioned on parity
stem: For $X\sim Bin(3,1/2)$, find its law and variance conditional on an even count.
solution: Only zero and two are admissible. Their original masses are $1/8$ and $3/8$, totaling one half. The conditional masses are therefore $1/4$ and $3/4$, with mean $3/2$, second moment three and variance $3/4$. These moments match the original fair binomial, yet the conditional support is different. This reinforces that even matching both mean and variance does not identify a named family. Conditioning must be applied to each retained atom before computing centered moments.

title: A direct hypergeometric second factorial moment
stem: For a uniform n-subset of N objects with K marks, derive $E[X(X-1)]$ and use it to recover variance.
solution: For each ordered pair of distinct sample positions, both are marked with probability $K(K-1)/[N(N-1)]$ when $N>1$. There are $n(n-1)$ ordered pairs, so the falling-factorial moment is $n(n-1)K(K-1)/[N(N-1)]$. Add the mean $nK/N$ to get the second raw moment and subtract the squared mean. Simplification yields $n(K/N)(1-K/N)(N-n)/(N-1)$. Ordered pairs explain the absence of a factor one half; unordered pairs instead correspond to $\binom X2$.

title: A posterior rate mixture after no events
stem: A hidden Poisson parameter is one or three with equal prior weights. Given a zero count in one exposure, find the probability the parameter was one and the next equal-exposure expected count.
solution: The zero likelihoods are $e^{-1}$ and $e^{-3}$. Bayes normalization gives posterior low-rate weight $e^{-1}/(e^{-1}+e^{-3})=e^2/(e^2+1)$. If the next count is conditionally independent given the same hidden parameter, its predictive mean is $(e^2+3)/(e^2+1)$. This is below the prior mean two because a quiet exposure favors the low-rate regime. Independent increments conditional on an unknown shared rate do not imply unconditional independent observations. Resetting the hidden parameter between exposures would change the predictive update.

title: Repeated until a sampled batch is acceptable
stem: Independent batches each contain four fair trials. Continue sampling batches until a batch has at least two successes. Find the expected number of batches and expected total number of trials.
solution: One batch is acceptable with probability $1-P(X=0)-P(X=1)=1-1/16-4/16=11/16$. Independent batches create a positive geometric batch wait with mean $16/11$. Each batch always contains four trials, so total trials equal four times the batch count and have mean $64/11$. Stopping within a batch at the second success would be a different experiment. A deterministic batch cost can be multiplied outside expectation; a random cost dependent on acceptability needs more careful accounting.

title: Stop at the first success among a finite set
stem: A random permutation of N items contains exactly one mark. Compare its first-mark position law with an independent geometric wait of success probability $1/N$.
solution: The unique marked position is uniform on one through N. Its mean is $(N+1)/2$ and variance $(N^2-1)/12$. An independent replacement wait with probability $1/N$ instead has mean N, variance $N(N-1)$ and unbounded support. Both experiments have initial success probability $1/N$, but after a failed finite-population draw the success hazard rises to $1/(N-i+1)$. One initial probability does not determine a waiting-time law; how the population or trial process changes afterward matters.

title: Assess an approximation at impossible finite counts
stem: A binomial count has n trials, and a Poisson approximation uses parameter np. What should be reported for a requested probability above n?
solution: The exact binomial probability of a count above n is zero by support. The Poisson approximation assigns a positive tail there when np is positive, because its support is unbounded. If the task asks for the exact answer, report zero before computing any approximation. If it asks to study approximation quality, the Poisson tail is an explicit mismatch and contributes to total variation. An approximation does not alter the support of the original experiment. Absolute smallness may make the tail tolerable for some uses, but it cannot justify describing it as exact.
